summary: Checkpoint trimming preserves envelope-sealing progress and drains tombstoned rows even when the initial chunk budget expires

replay.detail: The first sealing pass after each open searches retained, untombstoned claims for missing source envelopes and rewinds only to the first affected batch. Recovery then commits its cursor in existing 64-batch chunks and resumes after restart. Daemon startup restores all signing credentials before writes and activates retained history after both API listeners bind. No graph projection replay is added. Existing unsigned member envelopes are signed in pages of at most 64 with signatures prepared off the writer and writer loans released between pages.

schema.detail: No table, column or index changes. Transactional batch_rowid_high_water metadata prevents reuse of deleted batch keys in both local append and peer admission.

rules.detail: Checkpoint rules, proof invariants, certificates and manifests are unchanged.

compatibility.detail: Batch rowids are local scan keys and are not part of signed batch or envelope identities. Older peers retain the same wire protocol.

downtime.detail: Normal daemon restart. Missing-envelope search and history sealing run after both API listeners bind; a store without skipped claims preserves its saved cursor and performs no recovery chunks. The first reader search may take about eight seconds on a million-batch store; concurrent sealing requests wait for it. Read requests retain their normal cancellation/deadline and pairing writes retain their acknowledgement semantics.

manual.detail: No manual repair. Reachable-member read-only counts found zero retained claims without a source envelope or a claim tombstone.

recovery.detail: Deploy forward. An older writer can reintroduce rowid reuse and skipped envelope sealing after checkpoint deletion. Trimming now proves row exhaustion with a lookup before marking completion, including when chunk setup spends its budget. A subsequent upgrade detects retained batches skipped by an older writer during a downgrade.
